candidates.title: A lawyer used AI to write a report, but billed full time. What should I do?
candidates.raw_content: This is not a request for legal advice, and therefore the country matters little here. I write because I am interested in hearing opinions on the moral implications of something that is bound to happen more and more often. Context: A lawyer wrote a report for me. Not only was it was of poor quality, but he billed a surprising number of hours for it. I then noticed that one of the references was completely made up, typical of AI hallucination. I started pulling on the thread and slowly became convinced that he had almost certainly heavily relied on AI and inflated his hours. We went to the first judicial level, and the judge rejected out of hand the various strands of evidence that I presented. I feel like the deck is stacked against me (the lawyer also holds several prestigious positions), so I don't think I'll appeal. The risk is too high. However, Pangram since burst onto the scene, and essentially confirmed my suspicions (it flagged 1/3rd of the report as AI-generated, including the hallucinated reference). I know that the false-positive rate is higher for legal text, but I'm nonetheless more convinced than ever that I am correct in my assessment. What would you do in this situation? I'm annoyed that he got away with it, and that I don't have the time or the finances required to prove it. Comments URL: https://news.ycombinator.com/item?id=50468434 Points: 3 # Comments: 3

candidates.title: Show HN: Turri – a coding agent with the power of regenerative software
candidates.raw_content: Coding agents let me move fast. To keep up, I stopped reading the code, and with it I stopped understanding my own software. I lost my sense of engineering along with it. I was still the one accountable for software I didn't understand. No workflow or better model fixed that, so I built turri. turri is based on Pi and the concept of regenerative software introduced by Chad Fowler. The ability to regenerate the same piece of code multiple times and always get the same results in terms of functionality is called the deletion test and proves that your coding agent completely understands you. The idea is that every time part of the software needs to be changed, you regenerate a new version of the code based on the durable information you have about the system. The durable system information includes specs, tests, ADRs, and other types of documents, and it is written in ***plain. You write these with the help of an agent, and Turri starts partial regeneration of the software you're changing. You can repeat this process as many times as you want until you're happy with the change you're implementing. The regeneration also includes proofs that the generated code completely conforms to the system knowledge on which it was based (it implements all the tests that are part of the definition and automatically adds additional tests). You can try this by cloning the repo or by installing it from my landing page. I created a desktop app to improve usability. Currently, it's only suitable for new projects, but I'm working on adding support for existing projects. I also wrote the full story in case you're interested: https://turri.dev/blog/why-i-built-turri/ Comments URL: https://news.ycombinator.com/item?id=50468121 Points: 5 # Comments: 3

candidates.title: I scraped 803 companies sub-processors to investigate what AI native companies are using for their infrastructure.. Some interesting findings from the last time I did this in March: > 44% of companies list two+ model providers (up from 33%). Small n, but Anthropic grew twice as fast as OpenAI. > 86 pairs where each company names the other as a subprocessor (@AnthropicAI + @Cloudflare, @vercel + @spacexai) > 33% of companies list an inference provider (up from 22%). @modal continues to crush. > Chinese models are primarily coming through video (think Bytedance) rather than text (at least on the subprocessor lists) > @typesafeai is the breakout hit, going from 0 to many companies in a short period. Caveat: subprocessor lists tend to be a lagging indicator, but a sure shot way of knowing if the company is using something. You can find all the updated data, design and insights at deploygraph dot com. Feedback welcome!

candidates.title: There are basically two kinds of companies to build right now. 1. Diffusion of AI This is the "vertical SaaS" of today. There are a bunch of different models for it (FDE company, rollup, horizontal product) but ultimately it all boils down to the same thing: get AI diffused very close to where the work is being done. Profound, Cognition, Harvey etc. A lot of great companies will get built here. 2. Frontier of AI This is where the really interesting action is. Use AI to accelerate scientific progress, then build products from that progress. It is a harder category to see. But we are seeing a lot more of it at @spc: - Externa is adding hundreds of new chemical building blocks to proteins, so you can engineer a drug to match the disease instead of settling for what nature gave you. - Epana Bio is using genomics and AI to design autoimmune therapies that go after the cellular origin of the disease. - VenomicsAI is doing AI-accelerated drug discovery from venoms. - Equivariant is doing multi-physics modeling for the semiconductor industry. (There are always picks-and-shovels for AI as well. Lots of amazing companies in that category.) Category 2 is not well understood or much talked about externally. It should be because I think that is where the vast majority of model driven returns will come from.

candidates.title: I look at what I do with Fable 5.2 in the cracks of my week and think: this would've taken five people and $200,000. Then I look at what my team does with the same AI. Last week, between meetings, I analyzed our customer survey, made a game for our team, spotted an opportunity to sell @Every to teams, built a CRM, and started reaching out. Look at that and you might ask: Why would I need a team at all? The chart seems to agree. On OpenAI's GDPval benchmark, AI went from beating human experts 12.4% of the time in 2024 to around 83% in 2026. That's the aggregate view of the future of work: gather a lot of data and extrapolate a trend line. But the aggregate misses something. To see it, you have to get intimate: zoom in on one real situation, with all its messiness, and extrapolate from there. We gave everyone at Every access to the same customer survey and the same AI models. • I found an opportunity to sell to teams. • @poojary_yash saw that first-time subscribers were churning because we send too much email. • @dabrundage noticed that many of our readers feel lonely: they're excited about AI, but people around them think they're crazy. • @jackcheng turned the results into a Claymation game show. Could you ask Claude to produce what each of them found? Maybe. But generating possibilities is cheap. Knowing which ones matter is hard. @hammer_mt ran an experiment to predict what I'd say in Slack. When Claude got 400 attempts, it produced an answer like mine 93% of the time. But when it had to rank its own answers, mine landed in its top 10% only around 60% of the time. Each person on a team is responsible for a different part of the world. That responsibility narrows where they look, and their perspective helps them decide what matters enough to act on. A team explores more possibilities than a single default prompt, and it can take responsibility for what it finds. The obvious objection: models will get better at ranking. I think they will. But people aren't frozen while that happens. Comparing 2026 Yash with 2027 Claude misses that there will also be a 2027 Yash, with another year of experience, using 2027 Claude. As models improve and spread, they raise the floor for everyone. The default answer becomes the baseline. The value is in using your perspective and responsibility to push past it. That's why I think we need to change how we measure AI. Instead of only asking how well a model performs on problems everyone agrees are worth solving, ask: How good is it at doing my work, from my perspective? The aggregate can show us the capability curve. The intimate helps us see what we might build, and who we might become, as we ride it. I presented this at Thesis: 2027. The full talk is on the Every podcast:

The aggregate can show us the capability curve. The intimate helps us see what we might build, and who we might become, as we ride it. I presented this at Thesis: 2027.
